rows.subtype: Approach: adjust routines to reduce stress while waiting [Revision]
rows.description: The person notices that scrolling at night raises fear, so sets a fixed sleep time, walks daily and limits searching to one short session. Managing mood and energy is part of coping with a wait.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, contingency planning, inversion, seeking advice

rows.subtype: Approach: follow the treatment plan with a reminder routine [Action]
rows.description: After a diagnosis, the person notes the doctor's instructions, sets phone reminders for appointments and tests, and keeps a folder of reports. Routines help carry out what the doctor advised.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, contingency planning, inversion, seeking advice

rows.subtype: Approach: rely on a home remedy from a relative instead of a check-up [Pitfall]
rows.description: A relative suggests a herbal remedy and reassures the person that it is nothing. The person delays medical care because the advice feels comforting rather than reliable.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: avoidance and procrastination, contingency planning, forward planning, inversion

rows.subtype: Approach: notice the pattern through a mood diary [Thinking]
rows.description: A final-year student who feels flat for weeks jots down sleep, appetite and mood each day, and sees a link with late nights and isolation. Writing makes the pattern visible and gives something concrete to share with a professional.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: tell a trusted friend or family member [Action]
rows.description: The student tells a close friend and later a sister that things have felt heavy for a month. Saying it aloud reduces isolation and brings in someone who can help with next steps.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: emotion-aware planning, forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: book an appointment with a counsellor or psychiatrist [Action]
rows.description: Using the college counselling centre or a helpline recommended by a doctor, the person books a session and writes a short summary of symptoms to share. Professional help is treated as a normal step, not a sign of weakness.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: emotion-aware planning, forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: push through and hide it [Pitfall]
rows.description: Believing that admitting struggle looks weak, the person keeps a cheerful face, skips meals and stops replying to friends. Suppression drains energy and delays help.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: emotion-aware planning, forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: cut all plans down to a minimum routine [Thinking]
rows.description: On low days the person sets only three tasks: wake at a set time, eat properly and step outside for ten minutes. Shrinking demands protects energy when big goals feel impossible.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: emotion-aware planning

rows.subtype: Approach: rely on one person as the only support [Pitfall]
rows.description: The student leans wholly on one roommate for every low moment, and the roommate becomes overwhelmed and withdraws. A single point of support is fragile and can strain the relationship.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: emotion-aware planning, forward planning

rows.subtype: Approach: build a wider support net with roles [Revision]
rows.description: After the roommate's fatigue, the student adds a counsellor, a weekly call with family and a walking group, and agrees with each on how they can help. Spreading support makes it sturdier.
graph_context: same problem, other approaches: emotion-aware planning, forward planning
